summary.text: Introducing \(I_n=\int_0^1(x(1-x))^n e^x\,dx\), an integration-by-parts recurrence shows that the odd-index linear error is \(b_{2n+1}-e a_{2n+1}=(-1)^n I_{n+1}/(n+1)!\); since \(0\le I_n\le e-1\) and the denominators are positive, the odd subsequence converges to \(e\). The recurrences also give the cross-determinant \(b_{2n+2}a_{2n+1}-a_{2n+2}b_{2n+1}=(-1)^{n+1}\), whose quotient by the growing denominator product tends to zero, so the even subsequence has the same limit and hence so does the full sequence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A_n=A340738(n),\qquad B_n=A340737(n),
\]
so that \(A_n\) is the denominator sequence and \(B_n\) is the corresponding numerator sequence. We include the harmless index-zero values
\[
A_0=B_0=0,
\]
and the initial values are
\[
A_1=1,\quad A_2=2,\qquad B_1=3,\quad B_2=5.
\]
Both sequences obey the same parity-dependent recurrence. It is convenient to write that recurrence with the indices already separated by parity. For every \(k\geq 0\), either sequence \(f=A\) or \(f=B\) satisfies
\[
f_{2k+3}=2f_{2k+2}+(2k+3)f_{2k+1},                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
f_{2k+4}=(k+3)f_{2k+3}-f_{2k+2}-(k+1)f_{2k+1}.                            \tag{2}
\]
These are precisely the odd and even cases of the defining recurrence.

We prove that
\[
\frac{B_n}{A_n}\longrightarrow e
\]
as \(n\to\infty\). All ratios below are regarded as real numbers.

## 1. Useful consequences of the recurrence

Substituting (1) into (2) gives a subtraction-free formula for the next even term:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{2k+4}
&=(k+3)\bigl(2f_{2k+2}+(2k+3)f_{2k+1}\bigr)
   -f_{2k+2}-(k+1)f_{2k+1}\\
&=(2k+5)f_{2k+2}+2(k+2)^2f_{2k+1}.                         \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, no truncation issue from subtraction in the natural-number recurrence remains in this formula: the displayed expansion shows that the quantity from which the two terms are subtracted is large enough, and the result is the nonnegative expression on the right.

We also obtain a recurrence involving only odd-indexed terms. Apply (1) with \(k+1\), then use (3):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{2k+5}
 &=2f_{2k+4}+(2k+5)f_{2k+3}\\
 &=2\bigl((2k+5)f_{2k+2}+2(k+2)^2f_{2k+1}\bigr)
   +(2k+5)f_{2k+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (1) once more to eliminate \(f_{2k+2}\), a direct simplification yields
\[
f_{2k+5}=(4k+10)f_{2k+3}+f_{2k+1}.                         \tag{4}
\]
Thus both \(A\) and \(B\) have the same second-order recurrence on their odd-indexed subsequences.

We next record the positivity and growth needed to ensure that denominators do not vanish. More generally, suppose a natural-number sequence \(f\) satisfies (1) and (3), with \(f_1\geq1\) and \(f_2\geq1\). We claim that for every \(k\geq0\),
\[
f_{2k+1}\geq k+1,\qquad f_{2k+2}\geq1.                    \tag{5}
\]
For \(k=0\), this is exactly the assumption on \(f_1,f_2\). If it holds for \(k\), then (1) gives
\[
f_{2k+3}=2f_{2k+2}+(2k+3)f_{2k+1}\geq k+2,
\]
and (3) gives
\[
f_{2k+4}=(2k+5)f_{2k+2}+2(k+2)^2f_{2k+1}\geq1.
\]
This completes the induction. In particular, since \(A_1=1,A_2=2\),
\[
A_{2k+1}\geq k+1,
\qquad A_{2k+2}\geq1.                                      \tag{6}
\]
The same conclusion also holds for \(B\), although only the denominator bounds in (6) will be needed below.

## 2. An integral recurrence

For \(j\geq0\), define
\[
I_j=\int_0^1 \bigl(x(1-x)\bigr)^j e^x\,dx.
\]
The integrand is continuous. On \([0,1]\), one has
\[
0\leq x(1-x)\leq1,
\]
and \(e^x>0\). Consequently
\[
0\leq I_j\leq \int_0^1e^x\,dx=e-1.                         \tag{7}
\]
The first two values are
\[
I_0=e-1                                                     \tag{8}
\]
and
\[
I_1=3-e.                                                    \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, (8) follows by integrating \(e^x\), while
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left((-x^2+3x-3)e^x\right)=x(1-x)e^x.
\]
Evaluating this antiderivative at \(1\) and \(0\) gives \(-e-(-3)=3-e\).

The key recurrence for these integrals is
\[
I_{j+2}=-2(j+2)(2j+3)I_{j+1}+(j+2)(j+1)I_j.                 \tag{10}
\]
To prove it, put \(u=x(1-x)\), so that \(u'=1-2x\), and consider
\[
F_j(x)=\left(u^{j+2}-(j+2)(1-2x)u^{j+1}\right)e^x.
\]
A direct differentiation using \(u'=1-2x\) gives
\[
F_j'(x)=
\left(
 u^{j+2}+2(j+2)(2j+3)u^{j+1}-(j+2)(j+1)u^j
\right)e^x.                                                 \tag{11}
\]
For completeness, this is obtained by differentiating the bracket and then adding the bracket itself because \((e^x)'=e^x\). After factoring out \(u^j\), the resulting polynomial identity in \(x\) simplifies to the expression in (11).

At both endpoints \(x=0\) and \(x=1\), we have \(u=0\). Since the powers occurring in \(F_j\) are \(j+1\) and \(j+2\), both positive, it follows that
\[
F_j(0)=F_j(1)=0.
\]
Integrating (11) from \(0\) to \(1\), the integral of the derivative is therefore zero. By linearity of the integral,
\[
I_{j+2}+2(j+2)(2j+3)I_{j+1}-(j+2)(j+1)I_j=0,
\]
which is equivalent to (10).

Now define the rescaled integral sequence
\[
T_k=\frac{(-1)^k}{(k+1)!}I_{k+1}.                            \tag{12}
\]
Taking \(j=k+1\) in (10) gives
\[
I_{k+3}=-2(k+3)(2k+5)I_{k+2}+(k+3)(k+2)I_{k+1}.
\]
Divide by \((k+3)!=(k+3)(k+2)(k+1)!\) and account for the alternating signs in (12). The result is
\[
T_{k+2}=(4k+10)T_{k+1}+T_k.                                 \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(T_k\) satisfies exactly the same recurrence as the odd-indexed subsequences in (4).

Its first two values are also important. From (9),
\[
T_0=I_1=3-e.                                                 \tag{14}
\]
To calculate \(T_1\), use (10) with \(j=0\):
\[
I_2=-12I_1+2I_0=-12(3-e)+2(e-1)=14e-38.
\]
Therefore
\[
T_1=-\frac{I_2}{2}=19-7e.                                   \tag{15}
\]
Finally, (7) and (12) imply
\[
|T_k|=\frac{I_{k+1}}{(k+1)!}
\leq \frac{e-1}{(k+1)!}
\leq \frac{e-1}{k+1}.                                      \tag{16}
\]
Here \((k+1)!\geq k+1\), and \(e-1\geq0\).

## 3. Identification of the odd-index error

Define
\[
S_k=B_{2k+1}-eA_{2k+1}.
\]
Applying (4) separately to \(A\) and \(B\) and subtracting \(e\) times the recurrence for \(A\) from the recurrence for \(B\), we obtain
\[
S_{k+2}=(4k+10)S_{k+1}+S_k.                                 \tag{17}
\]
The initial values agree with those of \(T\). Indeed,
\[
S_0=B_1-eA_1=3-e=T_0.
\]
Also, by the odd recurrence (1),
\[
A_3=2A_2+3A_1=7,
\qquad
B_3=2B_2+3B_1=19,
\]
so
\[
S_1=19-7e=T_1.
\]
The recurrences (13) and (17), together with these two initial equalities, prove by induction that
\[
B_{2k+1}-eA_{2k+1}=S_k=T_k                              \tag{18}
\]
for every \(k\geq0\).

Since \(A_{2k+1}>0\) by (6), division by it is legitimate. From (18),
\[
\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}-e=\frac{T_k}{A_{2k+1}}.
\]
Moreover, \(A_{2k+1}\geq k+1\geq1\), so (16) gives the simple bound
\[
\left|\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}-e\right|
=\frac{|T_k|}{A_{2k+1}}
\leq |T_k|
\leq \frac{e-1}{k+1}.                                      \tag{19}
\]
The right-hand side tends to zero. Hence
\[
\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}\longrightarrow e.                \tag{20}
\]
This proves convergence along the odd indices.

## 4. The determinant identity and the even indices

To compare each even-indexed fraction with the preceding odd-indexed fraction, define the integer determinant
\[
E_k=B_{2k+2}A_{2k+1}-A_{2k+2}B_{2k+1}.                      \tag{21}
\]
We show that
\[
E_{k+1}=-E_k.                                                \tag{22}
\]
There is a transparent matrix interpretation. For either sequence \(f=A\) or \(f=B\), formulas (1) and (3) say
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
f_{2k+4}\\
f_{2k+3}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2k+5 & 2(k+2)^2\\
2 & 2k+3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
f_{2k+2}\\
f_{2k+1}
\end{pmatrix}.                                               \tag{23}
\]
The determinant of the transition matrix is
\[
(2k+5)(2k+3)-4(k+2)^2=-1.                                   \tag{24}
\]
The quantity \(E_k\) is the determinant formed from the corresponding \(B\)- and \(A\)-vectors. Applying the same matrix in (23) to both vectors multiplies this determinant by the determinant of the matrix, namely \(-1\). This proves (22).

At \(k=0\),
\[
E_0=B_2A_1-A_2B_1=5\cdot1-2\cdot3=-1.
\]
It follows inductively from (22) that
\[
E_k=(-1)^{k+1},
\qquad |E_k|=1.                                              \tag{25}
\]

Both denominators in the following computation are positive by (6). Subtracting adjacent fractions and using (21), we find
\[
\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}-
\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}
=
\frac{E_k}{A_{2k+2}A_{2k+1}}.
\]
By (6),
\[
A_{2k+2}A_{2k+1}\geq 1\cdot(k+1)=k+1.
\]
Together with (25), this gives
\[
\left|
\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}-
\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}
\right|
\leq \frac1{k+1}.                                           \tag{26}
\]
Using the triangle inequality and then (19) and (26),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}-e\right|
&\leq
\left|
\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}-
\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}
\right|
+
\left|\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}-e\right|\\
&\leq \frac1{k+1}+\frac{e-1}{k+1}.
\end{aligned}                                                \tag{27}
\]
The right-hand side tends to zero, so
\[
\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}\longrightarrow e.                \tag{28}
\]
Thus the even-indexed subsequence has the same limit.

## 5. Recombining the two parity subsequences

It remains only to pass from (20) and (28) to the entire sequence. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By (20), there is \(N_1\) such that for every \(k\geq N_1\),
\[
\left|\frac{B_{2k+1}}{A_{2k+1}}-e\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
By (28), there is \(N_2\) such that for every \(k\geq N_2\),
\[
\left|\frac{B_{2k+2}}{A_{2k+2}}-e\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
Choose a sufficiently large integer \(M\), for example
\[
M=2(N_1+N_2)+2.
\]
If \(m\geq M\), there are two cases. If \(m\) is odd, then \(m=2k+1\); the lower bound on \(m\) forces \(k\geq N_1\), so the first estimate applies. If \(m\) is even, then \(m=2k+2\); the same lower bound forces \(k\geq N_2\), so the second estimate applies. Thus every sufficiently late term, regardless of parity, lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(e\).

Consequently
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{A340737(n)}{A340738(n)}=e}.
\]
The artificially included index-zero value has no effect on this limiting statement.
